content: The Plague of Cyprian refers to a pandemic, likely caused by smallpox, that afflicted the Roman Empire starting in 251 AD. This outbreak persisted for decades and was still active in 270 AD, during which it claimed the life of Emperor Claudius II Gothicus, who ruled from 268 to 270 AD. The pandemic led to significant manpower shortages, particularly in agriculture and the Roman military. The plague is named after Saint Cyprian, an early Christian writer who documented and described the outbreak. At the height of the epidemic, between 251 and 266 AD, it was reported that as many as 5,000 people per day were dying in Rome. Pontius the Deacon, Cyprian’s biographer, wrote about the plague’s impact in Carthage, noting that Christians were scapegoated during the Decian persecution, much like Jews were blamed during the Black Death in the 14th century. Approximately fifty years later, Arnobius, a North African convert to Christianity, defended his faith against pagan accusations. Cyprian himself used the plague as a moral and theological teaching point in his sermons to the Christian community. He also provided a vivid description of the symptoms in his essay De Mortalitate (On the Plague). Historian William McNeill has suggested that the Antonine Plague and the Plague of Cyprian were caused by two distinct diseases, one being smallpox and the other measles, though the order of these outbreaks remains uncertain. The severe impact of these plagues on the European population suggests that the people of the time had no prior exposure or immunity to these diseases. However, the prevailing modern consensus is that both outbreaks were caused by smallpox.
